attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: The first clause ('no immediate fix in the offing') is a firm near-term assertion. The second clause ('not certain we will see one soon') is hedged and cannot be scored. The proposition's 'may not arrive soon' keeps the hedge, but the modality tag 'unlikely' is a bit stronger than 'not certain'.

contract.note: The contract scores only the firm clause and sets no deadline, since 'immediate' and 'soon' give none. It defines a 'fix' as broad elimination of hallucinations, which is a fair ordinary reading. Under this deadline-free reading, later persistence of hallucinations cannot settle the claim.

evidence.note: May 2024 preregistered study: legal RAG tools still hallucinated 17–33% of the time. This fits 'no immediate fix', but the contract says later persistence cannot conclusively support the claim.
June 2024 Nature paper on semantic entropy. It detects a subset of hallucinations (confabulations) and does not eliminate them, so it is partial progress, not a qualifying fix.

reviews.rationale: The firm clause is a deadline-free near-term forecast. Nothing in the packet shows a broad, independently validated fix at or right after publication, so the early contradiction rule is not met. The later evidence shows hallucinations persisting, which fits the claim but cannot conclusively support it under the contract. The hedged second clause is not scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: This is a present-state observation with two parts (no profits, no moat). The 'at least so far' qualifier is kept as a condition.

contract.note: Reading 'profits' as company-wide net earnings and 'moat' as a durable competitive advantage is ordinary. Using calendar 2023 is a reasonable choice of period, although 'so far' could also be read as cumulative. Requiring a matching accounting basis is strict but does not change the result here.

evidence.note: Secondary report of a $540M loss in 2022. That is a different period from the 2023 target and the accounting measure is unspecified, so it is context only.
Google's own disclosure about launching Gemini. It shows competition exists but does not show whether OpenAI had a durable advantage.
LMSYS ranking as of Jan 26, 2024: GPT-4 Turbo first, Bard second. A temporary leaderboard position neither proves nor rules out a moat.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no 2023 company-wide net-earnings figure; the only loss figure covers 2022. The competitive evidence shows rivals and a mixed benchmark picture, but it does not establish whether OpenAI had a durable moat. Neither part of the claim can be settled from this evidence.

attribution.note: Marcus's own characterization of OpenAI's position, in his own post.

semantics.note: The claim joins a testable fact (licensing was available) with Marcus's characterization that OpenAI framed free use as the only option. 'False dichotomy' is evaluative, but both parts underneath it can be checked.

contract.note: The contract splits the claim into licensing availability and the characterization of OpenAI's submission, and allows a mixed verdict. It also does not require proof that every training input could be licensed. This is a fair reading of Marcus's words.

evidence.note: July 2023 AP announcement that OpenAI licensed part of AP's text archive. This shows a licensing route actually existed.

OpenAI's Dec 2023 submission, read from a third-party copy that the contract permits. It lists licensed third-party data among OpenAI's training sources, which undercuts the claim that OpenAI presented 'free' as the only option.

reviews.rationale: The licensing part holds: the AP deal shows licensing was available before the post. The characterization fails: the submission itself names licensed data as a training source, so it did not present free use as the sole option or leave licensing out. The contract assigns mixed when the two parts come out differently.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Revision 2 keeps his 'very difficult' wording rather than a firmer 'cannot'. This is a present-state observation.

contract.note: The ordinary reading is mixed accuracy plus no reliable way for users to spot errors, not that every answer is wrong. The contemporaneous period through January 2024 is appropriate.

evidence.note: Aug 2023 study: 52% of 517 ChatGPT programming answers were incorrect. In its 12-person user study, users often missed errors that were not obvious.
Jan 2, 2024 v1 of the legal study: 69–88% hallucination rates, and models often could not tell when they were hallucinating. It does not directly measure whether users detect errors.

reviews.rationale: Studies from the period show ChatGPT-era systems giving a mix of correct and incorrect answers. One user study shows people miss errors that are not obvious, and the legal study shows models lack a reliable confidence signal. Together these meet the support condition. The domain-specific rates are not generalized beyond their tasks.
